abstract: Proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9) is a secreted proprotein convertase that promotes lysosomal degradation of the hepatic low-density lipoprotein receptor (LDLR), thereby reducing the clearance of circulating low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C). Its validation as a therapeutic target is supported by human genetic evidence demonstrating that loss-of-function variants are associated with lifelong reductions in LDL-C and protection against cardiovascular disease. This review examines the biology of PCSK9 and the expanding range of strategies for its pharmacological inhibition, integrating evidence from human genetic studies, clinical trials, and preclinical models, with particular emphasis on translational relevance. The monoclonal antibodies evolocumab and alirocumab substantially reduce LDL-C levels and cardiovascular risk, whereas inclisiran, a small interfering RNA (siRNA), achieves sustained suppression of hepatic PCSK9 synthesis with infrequent dosing. Recent therapeutic advances include the FDA approvals of lerodalcibep, a third-generation injectable PCSK9 inhibitor, and enlicitide decanoate, an orally administered macrocyclic peptide inhibitor. In parallel, nanoparticle-based delivery systems, active PCSK9 vaccination, and CRISPR-based genome editing represent emerging therapeutic strategies that remain largely in preclinical development. Beyond cardiovascular disease, PCSK9 has been implicated in sepsis, cancer, and neurodegenerative, pulmonary, and autoimmune disorders, although the supporting evidence remains heterogeneous and predominantly preclinical. In oncology, experimental findings implicating PCSK9 in tumor immune evasion and modulation of responses to immune checkpoint blockade have prompted its clinical evaluation as a potential adjunct to anticancer therapy. Further prospective clinical studies are required to establish the efficacy and long-term safety of novel PCSK9-targeted approaches and determine whether their therapeutic potential translates into meaningful clinical benefits.

title: PCSK9 Inhibition in Transition: From Established Treatments to Emerging Therapeutic Approaches.

abstract: Circular RNAs (circRNAs) are increasingly implicated in cancer treatment resistance, but the strength of evidence differs markedly among reported candidates. Because recent reviews have already catalogued circRNA biology, resistance mechanisms, and therapeutic applications, this narrative review focuses on how directly individual findings are linked to response to a defined anticancer treatment. Evidence is interpreted at four levels: human treatment-response data, direct in vivo resistance models, direct resistant cell-line models, and resistance-relevant biology without direct treatment testing. Direct treatment-resistance evidence includes circAKT3 in cisplatin resistance, hsa_circ_0007919 in gemcitabine resistance, circCDYL2 (hsa_circ_0004087) in trastuzumab resistance, and circRNA-SORE in sorafenib resistance. Experimental checkpoint-blockade studies also implicate circFGFR1 and circIGF2BP3 in reduced anti-PD-1 efficacy, although direct therapeutic resensitization by selective inhibition of these circRNAs was not established in the cited experiments. By contrast, several proposed links involving DNA repair, metabolism, stemness, or ferroptosis remain biologically plausible but have not been validated as treatment-resistance mechanisms. This distinction also changes biomarker interpretation: most tissue- or extracellular-vesicle-associated circRNAs should currently be regarded as candidate biomarkers of treatment response rather than clinically validated predictive biomarkers. We summarize the available human evidence, analytical requirements, and potential uses of longitudinal monitoring. Therapeutically, back-splice-junction-specific small interfering RNAs, antisense oligonucleotides, and RNA-targeting CRISPR systems can in principle suppress endogenous resistance-promoting circRNAs, whereas replacement approaches may restore sensitizing circRNAs. These endogenous-targeting strategies remain predominantly preclinical, whereas engineered circRNA therapeutics and cancer vaccines constitute a distinct platform that has begun early clinical development. Because the evidence base is dominated by preclinical models and small or retrospective clinical cohorts, with heterogeneous assays and endpoints, no circRNA discussed here should yet be considered a clinically validated predictive biomarker or an established resistance-reversal target.

abstract: mRNA vaccines established scalable manufacturing and lipid nanoparticle (LNP) delivery for sequence-defined, non-integrating RNA medicines. In vivo CAR-T therapy repurposes this platform to generate CAR-positive lymphocytes after intravenous dosing, but its active product is a time-varying cell population rather than the injected RNA mass. This review critically examines the pharmacological sequence from biodistribution and cell-specific uptake to cytosolic RNA release, surface CAR expression, effector function, and disease response. The evidence comprises primary human T cells, mice, humanized mice, non-human primates, and 11 patients described in one correspondence and two meeting abstracts (as of July 2026). Matched studies show that receptor internalization can outweigh surface abundance, ligand density follows a non-monotonic relationship with delivery, and lipid chemistry and ligand presentation independently alter productive T-cell transfection. Preclinical models demonstrate transient CAR expression and target-cell depletion, whereas current human reports establish feasibility but not durable efficacy, a dose-response relationship, or the incidence of uncommon toxicities. We therefore distinguish administered dose, cell-resolved CAR-positive-cell exposure, and pharmacodynamic response, and propose their joint measurement as the basis for comparing platforms and selecting repeat-dose regimens.

title: From mRNA Vaccines to In Vivo CAR-T Therapy: RNA-LNP Design and the Pharmacology of CAR-Positive Cells.

abstract: Introduction: Next-generation malaria vaccines are urgently needed to provide greater efficacy and longevity. Antibodies targeting blood-stage merozoites can confer protection against clinical malaria through multiple Fc-mediated functions. In particular, merozoite surface protein 2 (PfMSP2) is a known target of protective antibodies that can clear merozoites via multiple antibody Fc-mediated functions, making it a highly promising vaccine candidate. Methods: We developed PfMSP2 as a self-amplifying RNA (saRNA) vaccine, which was successfully validated for in vitro expression in mammalian cells. Subsequently, the PfMSP2-saRNA was formulated as lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) and evaluated for immunogenicity in mice following a three-dose regimen comparing 1 μg and 10 μg doses. We evaluated the induction of antibodies with functional activities relevant to protective immunity. Results: Our PfMSP2-saRNA vaccine induced antigen-specific IgG responses that recognised the surface of whole merozoites. Both 1 μg and 10 μg dosing regimens induced comparable antibodies to PfMSP2, and responses were predominantly murine cytophilic IgG subclasses. These vaccine-induced antibodies demonstrated potent Fc-mediated functions, including complement fixation and binding of human Fcγ-receptor I (FcγRI), after only two doses, which remained consistent after the third dose. Conclusions: PfMSP2 is highly immunogenic using the saRNA vaccine platform in a potential dose-sparing regimen, and induces antibodies with multiple Fc-mediated functions associated with protective immunity in humans. This saRNA platform is a promising strategy to develop highly efficacious vaccines requiring lower and fewer doses.

title: Evaluating a Potential Dose-Sparing Self-Amplifying RNA Vaccine for Induction of Functional Antibodies to Blood-Stage Plasmodium falciparum Malaria.

abstract: Messenger RNA (mRNA) vaccines offer a flexible approach to colorectal cancer (CRC) immunotherapy, with applications ranging from postoperative residual disease to metastatic cancer. This narrative review examines antigen selection, RNA engineering, nanodelivery, and clinical development, drawing on literature available through 21 October 2026. Tumor-associated antigens, shared driver mutations, and personalized neoantigens offer different advantages in population coverage, specificity, and manufacturing. Their activity also depends on RNA chemistry and carrier design, including lipid composition, endosomal release, APC targeting, tissue distribution, stability, and repeated dosing. Early clinical studies have demonstrated antigen-specific T-cell responses in selected patients, while randomized melanoma data provide a benchmark for combining vaccination with checkpoint blockade. The termination of the CRC adjuvant autogene cevumeran monotherapy trial highlights the difficulty of translating immune priming into recurrence prevention. Antigen heterogeneity, impaired HLA presentation, stromal exclusion, and liver-associated immune suppression remain important barriers in CRC. Advances in neoantigen prediction, self-amplifying RNA, and mechanism-based combinations may improve vaccine design, but their clinical value will depend on disease-specific trials that account for manufacturing feasibility and established oncological endpoints. The available evidence remains heterogeneous, with small CRC cohorts and limited randomized outcomes; the non-systematic search also introduces potential selection bias.

abstract: Yeast platforms are rapidly transitioning from traditional eukaryotic model organisms to versatile, programmable chassis for next-generation human health applications. This review systematically examines the translational evolution of conventional and non-conventional yeasts including Saccharomyces cerevisiae, Komagataella phaffii, Saccharomyces boulardii, and Yarrowia lipolytica and redefines them as scalable biomanufacturing factories and advanced living therapeutics. We highlight milestone advancements in synthetic biology toolkits that lower technical barriers, such as CRISPR-mediated multiplex editing, modular cloning frameworks, and high-throughput secretion screening. We focus on sophisticated glycoengineering strategies for humanized N-glycosylation, alongside data-driven paradigms that leverage artificial intelligence to predict gene expression and streamline strain design. In clinical domains, we detail the established success of yeast in producing subunit or virus-like particle vaccines (e.g. HBV and HPV) and therapeutic enzymes (e.g. ecallantide), alongside its emerging role as gut-adapted live biotherapeutic products (LBPs) engineered for in situ delivery and biosensing. Finally, we explore specialized non-conventional platforms, focusing on lipid- and acetyl-CoA-rich hosts for lipophilic drug discovery, and stress-tolerant systems optimized for economical, feedstock-flexible bioprocesses. In summary, this review underscores the integrated value of yeast systems across disease modeling, industrial manufacturing, and clinical intervention, charting future directions to address global health challenges.

abstract: Plasmacytoma variant translocation 1 (PVT1), a non-protein coding gene, is overexpressed in aggressive prostate cancer (PCa). Overexpression of PVT1 exon 9 has been demonstrated to induce malignant transformation of prostate epithelial cells and the development of aggressive PCa in vivo. However, the factors regulating overexpression and consequent oncogenicity of PVT1 exon 9 remain unclear. Here, we report the identification and functional characterization of a previously unrecognized internal regulatory element, the PVT1 exon 9 associated promoter (PEAP). We also demonstrate that its activity is governed by the caudal homeobox transcription factor CDX1 and local DNA methylation dynamics. While enzymatic methyl-sequence (EM-seq) profiling of PCa tissues and matched adjacent normal tissues revealed hypomethylation at PEAP in tumors, TFBind-based transcription factor motif prediction analysis revealed a discrete high-affinity CDX1 binding motif within PEAP. Using luciferase reporter assays, siRNA knockdown, CUT&RUN, CRISPR-based perturbation, isoform-specific droplet digital and quantitative PCR, we validated that the CDX1 motif within PEAP is functionally required for PEAP-driven induction of the oncogenic PVT1 exon 9 transcript. Moreover, CDX1 expression was significantly higher in aggressive PCa tissues compared to matched adjacent normal tissues in correlation with increased CDX1 occupancy at PEAP. Also, we uncovered enrichment of CDX1 at PEAP in PVT1 exon 9 overexpressing PCa cell lines, and increased CDX1 expression across PCa models overexpressing PVT1 exon 9. Targeting the predicted CDX1 binding motif within PEAP with a custom-designed antisense oligonucleotide disrupted CDX1 occupancy at PEAP, significantly inhibited expression of PVT1 exon 9, PCa cell proliferation and migration. Together, these results define a novel CDX1-PEAP signaling axis in which promoter methylation modulates CDX1 access to an internal regulatory element at PVT1, driving oncogenic PVT1 exon 9 overexpression. This work uncovers a novel regulatory mechanism in aggressive PCa and highlights the CDX1-PEAP axis as a potentially targetable node for therapeutic intervention in PVT1 exon 9 overexpressing aggressive PCa.

abstract: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) remains the leading cause of mortality worldwide and is associated with profound pathological remodeling at both the cellular and molecular levels. Beyond transcriptional changes, post-transcriptional regulation-including RNA splicing, modification, nuclear export, and degradation-significantly expands the complexity of the eukaryotic transcriptome. Among these processes, RNA degradation remains comparatively understudied in cardiovascular biology. Traditionally viewed primarily as a quality-control mechanism that removes aberrant transcripts, including those containing premature termination codons, RNA degradation is now increasingly recognized as an active regulatory process that controls RNA quality, transcript abundance, and ultimately gene expression under both physiological and pathological conditions. Multiple mechanisms regulate RNA stability and degradation, including nonsense-mediated mRNA decay, RNA modifications, RNA-binding proteins, and noncoding RNAs, particularly microRNAs. These pathways have been extensively implicated in biological and disease processes including cancer and inflammation, and emerging evidence highlights their importance in cardiovascular homeostasis and disease. In the heart, altered RNA stability and degradation contribute to the regulation of cardiac contractility, ion-channel homeostasis, mitochondrial function, and inflammatory response. Recent advances in reporter-based RNA stability assays and metabolic RNA-labeling approaches have further enabled quantitative measurement of RNA degradation both in vitro and in vivo. In this review, we summarize the molecular mechanisms regulating RNA stability and degradation, discuss their emerging roles in cardiovascular physiology and disease, highlight recent technological advances for studying RNA turnover, and examine therapeutic strategies targeting RNA stability. Together, these advances establish RNA degradation as an important and potentially druggable target in CVD.

abstract: Gain-of-function variants in KCNH1, which encodes the voltage-gated potassium channel Kv10.1, cause developmental and epileptic encephalopathies (DEEs) characterized by seizures, developmental delay and intellectual disability. While pathogenic variants enhance channel activity, loss of KCNH1 is tolerated in humans and mice, suggesting that allele-agnostic gene suppression may represent a viable therapeutic strategy. Here, we developed a gapmer antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) targeting KCNH1 and evaluated its efficacy in human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived neurons and a knock-in mouse model of KCNH1-related disorder. Neurons carrying the pathogenic KCNH1 variants I494V or G375R exhibited a shared phenotype characterized by hyperpolarized resting membrane potential and abnormalities in neuronal network activity despite largely preserved intrinsic firing properties. ASOs efficiently reduced KCNH1 expression without disrupting network activity in control neurons. In contrast, ASO treatment normalized network dysfunction across both mutant genotypes, demonstrating that distinct KCNH1 gain-of-function variants converge on a reversible disease state. To assess the efficacy of ASOs in vivo, we generated a new Kcnh1-R357Q knock-in mouse model that exhibited profound seizures and early mortality. A single ASO treatment reduced seizure burden significantly and restored survival to near-normal levels. Together, these findings establish KCNH1 suppression as a precision therapeutic strategy for KCNH1-related DEEs and provide a framework for treating gain-of-function epilepsies in which partial gene reduction is clinically tolerated.

abstract: Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) have rendered mRNA therapeutics clinically viable, yet their design remains impeded by tightly intertwined chemical, physical, biological, and manufacturing variables. This review argues that artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted LNP design should be approached as multiscale therapeutic-system engineering rather than reduced to isolated predictive tasks. We propose that AI models must holistically integrate ionizable lipid chemistry, supramolecular assembly, protein corona remodeling, endosomal escape, organ- and cell-specific tropism, cargo attributes, safety profiles, and process robustness into a cohesive framework. Current studies demonstrate that machine learning can prioritize ionizable lipids, predict formulation properties, guide tissue-selective delivery, and expedite the design-build-test-learn cycle. However, many models remain constrained by insufficient sample sizes, poor in vitro/in vivo translation, reliance on random-split validation, and narrow potency-centric endpoints. We propose and apply a claim-specific evidence hierarchy for AI-LNP studies and propose standardized multimodal datasets, mechanism-informed descriptors, scaffold-level holdout tests, and manufacturability-aware objective functions. We conclude that digital models of LNP delivery must be treated as emerging hypotheses until anchored by prospective and clinically relevant evidence.

title: AI-Assisted Lipid Nanoparticle Design for In Vivo mRNA Delivery: A Multiscale Therapeutic-System Engineering Framework.

abstract: The therapeutic potential of CRISPR/Cas genome editing has advanced the development of precision medicine; however, its clinical translation for many in vivo applications remains limited by challenges in achieving safe, efficient, and targeted delivery. Conventional viral vectors and synthetic nanocarriers are associated with challenges including immunogenicity, limited cargo capacity, prolonged nuclease expression, off-target effects, and manufacturing complexities. Engineered extracellular vesicles (EVs) are being investigated as alternative delivery carriers due to their biological origin, capacity for cargo encapsulation, and opportunities for surface functionalization. However, their biocompatibility, immunogenicity, and ability to cross biological barriers depend on vesicle source, formulation, and experimental conditions. This review provides a comprehensive overview of recent advances in the design of engineered EVs for CRISPR/Cas delivery, with a particular focus on strategies to improve cargo loading, targeting specificity, and therapeutic efficacy. We discuss the advantages and limitations of different CRISPR cargo formats, including plasmid DNA, mRNA, and ribonucleoprotein complexes, together with endogenous and exogenous loading approaches, hybrid EV platforms, and methods for enhancing intracellular delivery. Advances in EV surface engineering through genetic, chemical, physical, and biomimetic modifications are highlighted as strategies being investigated to improve tissue-specific delivery and functional cargo transport. The review also highlights emerging research directions, including CRISPR-EV theranostic platforms and the application of artificial intelligence to enhance CRISPR-EV therapeutic systems. Finally, key translational challenges, including scalable production, EV heterogeneity, cargo-loading efficiency, biodistribution, regulatory standardization, and quality control, are critically discussed. EV-mediated CRISPR delivery remains at an early preclinical stage, with clinical safety and therapeutic efficacy yet to be established. Further advances in EV engineering, cargo-loading strategies, and manufacturing standardization are needed to support its potential clinical translation.

title: Engineered Extracellular Vesicles (EVs) as Carriers for CRISPR/Cas9 Therapeutics: Recent Advances in Cargo Loading and Targeted Delivery.

abstract:
INTRODUCTION: The clinical success of mRNA vaccines during the COVID-19 pandemic accelerated the development of RNA-based therapeutics and validated their translational potential. This review examines recent advances and remaining challenges in the application of RNA technologies for cancer therapy.
AREAS COVERED: A literature search of PubMed, Web of Science, and Embase was conducted from database inception to July 2026. We review emerging RNA modalities, including messenger RNA, small interfering RNA, circular RNA, self-amplifying RNA, RNA editing technologies, and combinatorial RNA interference strategies for cancer treatment. Particular emphasis is placed on advances in delivery systems, including non-viral nanocarriers, exosomes, chemical modifications, and tumor-targeting approaches designed to improve stability, specificity, and therapeutic efficacy. Early clinical studies across solid and hematologic malignancies are also summarized.
EXPERT OPINION: RNA-based therapeutics have demonstrated encouraging preclinical and early clinical activity against cancer, but efficient and selective delivery remains the major barrier to broader clinical translation. The growing regulatory acceptance of RNA medicines and the adaptability of RNA design support the development of personalized therapies.Future advances will depend on improved delivery technologies, rational combination strategies, scalable manufacturing, and the integration of artificial intelligence to optimize RNA design and therapeutic development.

abstract: Mucopolysaccharidosis IVA (MPS IVA; Morquio A syndrome) is a lysosomal storage disorder caused by deficiency of N-acetylgalactosamine-6-sulfate sulfatase (GALNS), in which current therapies incompletely correct skeletal disease because enzyme delivery to avascular cartilage is limited. We developed a dual-lineage ex vivo gene-editing strategy combining murine hematopoietic stem/progenitor cells (mHSPCAAVS1) and rapidly expanding clonal human mesenchymal stem cells (REC-MSCs), using an integrase-defective lentiviral (IDLV) CRISPR/Cas9 platform designed to deliver a GALNS cassette to the AAVS1 safe-harbor locus. Nocodazole-mediated G2/M synchronization further increased GALNS output in HDR-competent conditions. Edited REC-MSCs showed supraphysiological GALNS production and secretion, and edited mHSPCAAVS1 reached approximately 13.9-fold wild-type activity; enhanced expression persisted at 30 days post-transduction. In non-contact transwell co-culture, edited REC-MSCs and edited mHSPCAAVS1 each increased GALNS activity in MPS IVA patient fibroblasts, and combined exposure produced the greatest correction, reducing lysosomal mass by ~36%, mono-sulfated keratan sulfate by ~54%, and mitochondrial superoxide toward wild-type levels at 30 days. Irradiated REC-MSC feeder layers supported 2.59-fold mHSPCAAVS1 expansion and a 1.96-fold higher proportion of EGFP-positive cells. Cross-correction was therefore achieved by each lineage and was greatest in combination, establishing a functional basis for in vivo evaluation of this dual-lineage strategy in MPS IVA.

abstract: Skin cancer represents a major global public health burden, with melanoma accounting for the majority of skin cancer-related mortality despite the higher prevalence of non-melanoma skin cancers such as basal cell carcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma. Ultraviolet radiation, genetic susceptibility, and lifestyle-related factors drive disease initiation and progression, underscoring persistent challenges in early diagnosis and durable therapeutic control, particularly in advanced and treatment-resistant disease. Emerging evidence identifies non-coding RNAs (ncRNAs)-including microRNAs, long non-coding RNAs, and circular RNAs-as critical regulators of oncogenic signalling pathways involved in proliferation, angiogenesis, epithelial-mesenchymal transition, immune evasion, and therapy resistance in skin cancer. Aberrant ncRNA expression patterns in tumor tissues and circulating biofluids are increasingly associated with disease stage, metastasis, and treatment response, highlighting their promise as diagnostic, prognostic, and predictive biomarkers. However, despite strong preclinical support, clinical translation of ncRNA-based therapeutics remains limited by challenges related to delivery efficiency, specificity, and safety. This review addresses a specific translational gap by integrating evidence on non-coding RNA (ncRNA) biology with nanoparticle-enabled delivery and CRISPR-based modulation in skin cancer. Particular emphasis is placed on distinguishing melanoma from non-melanoma skin cancers, evaluating ncRNAs according to their mechanistic and biomarker evidence, and critically assessing the preclinical and emerging clinical evidence for delivery and gene-modulation strategies. We further examine skin-specific delivery considerations, including topical and intratumoral administration, and discuss how nanoparticle platforms may facilitate localized delivery of ncRNA or CRISPR-associated cargos. Finally, we identify the major barriers to clinical translation, including biological heterogeneity, biomarker validation, delivery efficiency, off-target effects, immunogenicity, manufacturing complexity, and long-term safety, and propose an evidence-based framework for future precision oncology applications.

abstract: Diabetic retinopathy (DR), a prevalent microvascular complication, remains a leading cause of irreversible vision loss globally. Traditional DR managements, including anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) intravitreal injections, are limited by high treatment burden, suboptimal patient adherence, and transient efficacy. In recent years, gene therapy has represented a promising alternative, enabling long-term, adjustable, and endogenous production of therapeutic agents through a single administration. This review provides a comprehensive overview of the current understanding of DR from epidemiology, multimodal diagnosis, and molecular pathogenesis to the historical evolution and limitations of conventional therapies. Building upon these mechanistic insights, we further discuss recent advances in gene therapy for DR, extending beyond conventional anti-angiogenic strategies toward neurovascular unit protection, inflammation modulation, and metabolic regulation. Emerging gene-editing technologies, including Cas13-based RNA editing and prime editing (PE) for DNA correction, are also highlighted as promising next-generation therapeutic platforms. In addition, we summarized pioneering candidates in clinical trials, such as RGX-314, ADVM-022, and 4D-150, which have demonstrated promising efficacy in reducing the frequency of injections. Despite promising advances, we also discussed remaining challenges involving vector optimization, immune safety, transgene regulation, disease modeling, and patient stratification. Overall, gene therapy holds substantial potential to transform DR management from repetitive symptomatic intervention toward durable and personalized molecular treatment.

abstract: The establishment of endometrial receptivity is a sophisticated process essential for embryo attachment, invasion, and subsequent development, serving as the cornerstone for a healthy pregnancy. Impaired endometrial receptivity underlies diverse reproductive complications, underscoring the urgent need to elucidate its pathophysiological mechanisms and develop innovative pharmacological interventions. Recently, epigenetics has emerged as a focal point of scientific interest due to its critical contribution to the pathogenesis of reproductive disorders and the consequent advancement of precision therapies. Herein, we characterize the dynamic epigenetic landscapes of endometrium throughout the menstrual cycle and synthesize recent advances regarding how epigenetic modifications, including DNA methylation, RNA methylation, and histone modifications, orchestrate the establishment of endometrial receptivity. Moreover, we discuss prospective epigenetic drugs, such as the DNMT inhibitor AZA and HDAC inhibitor TSA, which exhibit therapeutic potential for improving endometrial receptivity. We also highlight CRISPR-based epigenome editing an emerging precision intervention and critically discuss current challenges in implementing these approaches. Taken together, these findings shed light on underlying molecular mechanisms and point toward promising avenues for translating epigenetically targeted therapies into clinical application to improve endometrial receptivity.

abstract: Background/Objectives: Myotonic dystrophy type 1 (DM1) is the most common form of adult-onset muscular dystrophy. DM1 is caused by a CTG trinucleotide repeat expansion in the 3'-untranslated region of the DMPK gene. Expanded CUG repeat RNA forms nuclear CUG RNA foci that sequester the RNA-binding protein MBNL1, leading to loss of MBNL1 function and resulting in splicing abnormalities. MBNL1 autoregulates its nuclear localization by repressing the inclusion of exon 5, which encodes part of its nuclear localization signal. In DM1, exon 5 inclusion is increased due to loss of MBNL1 function. However, whether inclusion of exon 5 contributes to the formation of nuclear CUG RNA foci remains unclear; we investigated this relationship in the present study. Methods: We used dCasRx, the catalytically inactive form of Cas13d, together with guide RNAs targeting sequences within and around exon 5 to identify an optimal sequence for exon 5 skipping. An antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) designated ex5-ASO, designed from the selected sequence, was transfected into a cellular DM1 model and DM1 patient-derived fibroblasts to assess their effects on RNA foci. Results: ex5-ASO successfully induced skipping of not only MBNL1 exon 5 but also MBNL2 exon 5 in a dose-dependent manner. The cytoplasmic fractions of both MBNL1 and MBNL2 increased following ex5-ASO transfection. Remarkably, ex5-ASO treatment reduced nuclear RNA foci and induced the appearance of cytoplasmic foci. However, despite reduced nuclear RNA foci and substantial residual nuclear MBNL1/2, mis-splicing persisted after ex5-ASO treatment. Conclusions: The level of MBNL1/2 exon 5 inclusion affects nuclear RNA foci formation, suggesting that the increased exon 5 inclusion observed in DM1 is not merely a consequence of MBNL loss of function but may also contribute to the nuclear accumulation of RNA foci and sequestration of MBNL1/2.

abstract: In this article we have reviewed potential therapeutic strategies relating to two of the primary coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10) deficiencies, COQ4 and COQ8A; these disorders have been grouped together because of their complimentary roles in stabilising the CoQ10 enzyme complex, Complex Q, as well as the difficulty in treating either of these disorders using conventional oral supplementation, as exemplified by two previously unreported case histories. Alternative strategies reviewed include methods to potentially improve blood-brain barrier access, including the identification of suitable inhibitors or activators of LRP1 or SRB1 transporters respectively. Other potential therapeutic strategies include the potential stabilisation of Complex Q using agents such as cardiolipin, targeted gene therapy using CRISPR/Cas9 gene-editing or AAV vector gene delivery, or mitochondrial transplantation. All of the strategies outlined above are at an early preclinical stage with regard to their potential application in primary CoQ10 deficiency, and remain areas for ongoing research.

abstract: Duchenne muscular dystrophy is caused by pathogenic variants in the DMD gene. Splice-site variants can generate aberrant transcripts whose consequences cannot always be predicted by the classical reading-frame rule. Here, we characterized the c.4675-2A>G variant at the exon 34 splice acceptor site for the development of an exon-skipping therapy. A minigene analysis demonstrated that c.4675-2A>G activated a cryptic splice acceptor within exon 34 rather than inducing skipping of the entire exon, resulting in deletion of the first 7 nucleotides, a frameshift, and a premature termination codon. To restore the reading frame by promoting skipping of the entire exon 34, we used antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) targeting distinct splice-regulatory regions. Among the ASO treatments tested, including individual ASOs and ASO combinations, A1&E4&D1 produced the highest exon exclusion and consistently promoted exon 34 skipping across the examined -2A mutant genotypes. A1&E4&D1 consists of ASOs A1, E4, and D1. A1 targeted the cryptic 3' splice acceptor region, E4 targeted a predicted exonic splicing enhancer region, and D1 targeted the 5' splice donor region. These findings illustrate a stepwise, variant-directed strategy in which characterization of aberrant splicing guides the design of a tailor-made ASO intervention.

title: The Need for Variant-Specific Splicing Assessment in Developing Antisense Oligonucleotide Therapies for Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy: Lessons from the DMD c.4675-2A>G Variant.

abstract: Cancer-associated metabolic reprogramming is a dynamic process that supports tumor growth, adaptation, and therapeutic resistance. Among the post-transcriptional mechanisms contributing to this plasticity, alternative splicing has emerged as an important regulator of glycolytic metabolism by generating transcript and protein isoforms with distinct biochemical and regulatory properties. This review examines the molecular mechanisms linking alternative splicing to cancer glycolysis, with particular emphasis on pyruvate kinase M1/pyruvate kinase M2 (PKM1/PKM2) isoform regulation as the best-characterized, but context-dependent, model of splice-associated metabolic control rather than as a universal tumor-specific switch. Additional splice-dependent mechanisms affecting glycolysis-related enzymes, transporters, receptors, and regulatory proteins further illustrate that the metabolic impact of alternative splicing extends beyond PKM and may influence glucose uptake, glycolytic enzyme activity, pyruvate fate, and lactate metabolism. The review further highlights the regulatory roles of key RNA-binding proteins and splicing factors, together with upstream oncogenic signaling pathways, in establishing cancer-associated splicing programs. Hypoxia, glucose and energy stress, lactate-dependent protein lactylation, and oxidative stress can modify spliceosomal activity and splicing-factor function, whereas extracellular acidosis is better regarded as a potential modulatory input whose independent role in splice-site selection remains less firmly established. Functionally, splicing-driven glycolytic remodeling contributes to tumor growth, metabolic adaptation, invasion, metastasis, cancer stemness, and therapy resistance. Therapeutically, the splicing-glycolysis axis may be exploited through modulation of the splicing machinery, antisense oligonucleotide-mediated splice switching, isoform-directed strategies, and combined or synthetic-lethal approaches targeting splice-induced metabolic dependencies. Future studies integrating isoform-resolved transcriptomics with proteomics, metabolomics, spatial and single-cell approaches, and metabolic flux analysis will be essential for distinguishing functionally relevant splice variants from non-functional transcript diversity and for identifying clinically actionable metabolic vulnerabilities.

title: Isoform Switching as a Regulatory Mechanism of Glycolytic Reprogramming in Cancer.

abstract: Huntington's disease (HD) is an autosomal dominant neurodegenerative disorder caused by a CAG repeat expansion in HTT. Despite its well-defined genetic cause, developing safe and effective disease-modifying therapies has remained challenging. By September 2026, the therapeutic landscape included regulatory submissions for the adeno-associated virus serotype 5 (AAV5)-delivered RNA interference therapy ifezuntirgene inilparvovec (AMT-130) and the discontinuation of tominersen after the GENERATION HD2 trial, in which target engagement and biomarker responses were achieved without clinical benefit. These contrasting developments highlight both the progress achieved and the challenges of translating molecular interventions into clinical benefit. Here, we review five complementary therapeutic strategies grounded in current understanding of HD pathogenesis: editing the HTT sequence or modifying its epigenetic regulation; suppressing somatic CAG expansion by modulating DNA repair; lowering huntingtin expression with antisense oligonucleotides, AAV-delivered RNA interference and oral splicing modulators; modifying mutant huntingtin aggregation and proteostasis; and targeting downstream pathological processes. Together, these advances support combination approaches targeting multiple pathogenic mechanisms, although their efficacy and safety remain to be established. More than three decades after the identification of the causative mutation, a deeper understanding of HD biology and expanding therapeutic approaches provide grounds for cautious optimism about meaningful improvements for people with HD.

title: Disease-Modifying Therapeutics for Huntington's Disease: State of the Art.

abstract: Gene therapy has emerged as a promising approach for the treatment and prevention of genetic disorders through targeted modification of cellular DNA. The clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats-CRISPR-associated protein 9 (CRISPR-Cas9) system, in particular, has enabled precise correction of disease-causing mutations. Recently, increasing interest has been directed toward in utero gene therapy, which offers a unique therapeutic window to prevent irreversible pathological changes before birth. This narrative review explores the current preclinical landscape of in utero CRISPR-Cas9-mediated genome editing. A literature search was conducted using PubMed/MEDLINE and Google Scholar databases to identify relevant studies, focusing primarily on delivery strategies, temporal considerations, therapeutic efficacy, and safety outcomes. Preclinical evidence demonstrates that prenatal delivery of CRISPR-Cas9 components in animal models can achieve durable genome editing in multiple fetal tissues, leading to phenotypic improvements in metabolic and early-onset lethal disorders. However, significant challenges remain, including off-target effects, mosaicism, maternal-fetal immune interactions, and the risk of unintended germline transmission. Ultimately, while in utero CRISPR-Cas9 gene therapy holds substantial therapeutic potential for severe congenital pathologies, rigorous safety evaluation, delivery optimization, and resolution of ethical and regulatory dilemmas are strictly required before clinical translation can be considered.

title: In Utero Gene Therapies Using CRISPR-Cas9 Technology: A Narrative Review of Current Research and Translational Perspectives.

abstract: Infectious bursal disease (IBD) is an acute, highly contagious, and immunosuppressive disease of poultry caused by the infectious bursal disease virus (IBDV). For more than 30 years, the very virulent IBDV (vvIBDV) characterized by high mortality has been widely prevalent worldwide, inflicting considerable economic losses on poultry-producing regions and thereby hampering the healthy development of the industry. However, the existing live vaccines carry the risk of restoring virulence and are susceptible to interference from maternal antibodies, while inactivated vaccines often result in insufficient protection. Therefore, it is urgent to develop novel vaccines with improved safety and efficacy. In this study, an mRNA vaccine encoding the VP2 protein of vvIBDV was developed for the first time. Efficient protein expression of mRNA-HLJVP2 was confirmed through in vitro transfection experiments. Immunization experiments in chickens demonstrated that the mRNA-HLJVP2-LNP with three different doses induced specific neutralizing antibodies and significantly increased the proportions of IL-4-secreting CD4+ T cells and IFN-γ-secreting CD8+ T cells. In the following challenge experiment, the mRNA-HLJVP2-LNP immunization groups exhibited good protective efficacy, with the single immunization group (20 μg dose) providing effective protection for chickens from death and bursa lesions induced by vvIBDV challenge. This study provides a promising candidate vaccine for the control of the vvIBDV and highlights its potential for clinical application in the prevention of IBD.

title: The mRNA-LNP Vaccine Encoding Viral VP2 Confers Effective Protection Against Very Virulent Infectious Bursal Disease Virus (vvIBDV).

abstract: Lipid nanoparticle (LNP)-mRNA vaccines compressed the path from pathogen sequence to licensed product into less than a year and are now approved for three viral diseases (COVID-19, respiratory syncytial virus and seasonal influenza), with more than twenty indications in clinical development. The platform's potency is no longer in doubt; its predictability is. We argue that progress is now limited by three interfaces that are engineered largely independently: the lipid-RNA interface, which sets encapsulation, internal structure and storage stability; the particle-cell interface, which sets tropism and the efficiency of endosomal escape; and the particle-immune interface, which sets the balance between adjuvanticity and reactogenicity. Quantitative design rules exist for the first interface, remain empirical for the second, and are almost absent for the third, which is why formulation development still proceeds by screening rather than by calculation. We review the molecular design of the mRNA payload and structural antigen selection; the chemistry, manufacture and intracellular trafficking of LNPs; the immunological chain that links innate activation and dendritic-cell cross-presentation to germinal-centre output; and the clinical evidence across COVID-19, respiratory syncytial virus, influenza, cytomegalovirus, HIV, personalised cancer vaccines and other targets. We conclude by identifying the measurements, pharmacopoeial quality attributes and design rules that would make the next generation of LNP-mRNA vaccines predictable rather than empirical.

title: Lipid Nanoparticle-mRNA Vaccines for Infectious Diseases: Making a Potent Platform Predictable.

abstract: Objectives: Over the past decades, lipid nanoparticle (LNP) technology has achieved remarkable success and has established itself as the predominant delivery system for mRNA vaccines and therapeutics. Despite their success, lipid-based mRNA delivery systems still face significant stability challenges and often require ultra-cold storage and transportation, which complicates global distribution and limits widespread patient access. Applying lyophilization to complex formulations such as LNPs requires rational process design and a clear understanding of critical process parameters and quality attributes. In this work, we focused on the impact of cryoprotectant selection and freezing conditions, with a particular focus on freezing as the first step of the freeze-drying cycle. Methods: We systematically evaluated the impact of well-established sugar-based cryoprotectants on the colloidal stability and biological performance of mRNA-loaded LNPs upon freezing and subsequent lyophilization. The freezing step, identified as the most critical process step in the lyophilization cycle, was investigated across multiple cooling rates to assess its effect on particle properties. Results: Under the conditions tested, sucrose better preserved mRNA-LNP properties than trehalose after freezing and lyophilization. The effects observed during freeze-thaw cycling depended on the selected cooling rate. In a broader sugar screen, formulations containing fructose-containing saccharides generally showed better preservation of colloidal properties after freeze-thaw cycling than the glucose-based comparators. Adding fructose to trehalose-containing formulations also reduced the changes observed after freeze-thaw cycling. Conclusions: Sugar selection and cooling conditions influence the response of the tested mRNA-LNP formulation to freezing. These findings support freeze-thaw testing as a formulation-screening approach but do not establish the molecular mechanism of sugar-mediated protection or the long-term storage stability of lyophilized LNPs.

title: The Interplay of Cooling Rates and Sugar Selection in mRNA-LNP Freezing and Lyophilization.

abstract: One approach to therapeutic cancer vaccine development uses whole tumor cells or their lysates as sources of a broad repertoire of tumor antigens. A key advantage of this strategy is that it does not require prior identification of tumor antigens, unlike personalized neoantigen peptide or mRNA vaccines, potentially reducing the time and cost of vaccine development. However, late-phase clinical trials have not demonstrated sufficient efficacy of tumor cell-based cancer vaccines. Currently, strategies to enhance the therapeutic potential of vaccines based on whole tumor cells and their derived lysates are being actively developed, and the vaccine potential of individual tumor cell components, such as cell membranes and extracellular vesicles, is under investigation. In this review, we systematize data on how whole tumor cells and their derivatives (lysates, cell membranes, and extracellular vesicles) are used to generate therapeutic cancer vaccines, analyze the results of experimental and clinical studies, and evaluate promising engineering and combination therapy strategies capable of overcoming the current limitations of this platform.

abstract: Self-incompatibility (SI) is a key reproductive barrier in citrus species that prevents self-fertilization and maintains genetic diversity. In pummelo (Citrus grandis L. Osbeck), SI is governed by an S-ribonuclease (S-RNase)-based gametophytic system, but the mechanisms underlying pollen tube rejection remain poorly understood. Here, we identified pollen-expressed arginine decarboxylase (ADC) as a non-S-locus factor that interacts with S-RNases and may contribute to pollen tube responses under S-RNase-associated stress. Phylogenetic and structural analyses indicated that CgADC belongs to the conserved plant arginine decarboxylase family. Molecular docking predicted a potential hydrophobic interaction interface between CgADC and S-RNase. Using yeast two-hybrid screening, split-luciferase complementation, pull-down assays, and subcellular localization, we found that CgADC associates with multiple S-haplotype S-RNases. CgADC transcripts were significantly more abundant under incompatible conditions, while recombinant CgADC exhibited enhanced enzymatic activity following S-RNase treatment in vitro. Antisense oligonucleotide-mediated suppression of CgADC expression significantly reduced pollen tube elongation. Exogenous recombinant CgADC partially alleviated pollen tube growth inhibition and was associated with changes in ROS-related fluorescence patterns. However, its uptake into the pollen tube cytoplasm was not directly demonstrated. Together, these findings identify CgADC as a potential non-S-locus factor associated with the pummelo SI response and suggest a link between S-RNase-associated responses, ADC activity, and ROS-related regulation.

title: S-RNase activates arginine decarboxylase to modulate redox responses during self-incompatibility in pummelo.

abstract: CRISPR-based genome/epigenome editing and RNA-targeted therapeutics offer unprecedented precision for correcting disease-causing mutations, yet clinical translation remains constrained by two unresolved bottlenecks: suboptimal guide RNA (gRNA) design limiting editing efficiency and specificity, and the absence of safe, tissue-selective delivery platforms. While machine learning (ML)-driven gRNA design and peptide-mediated delivery have each advanced substantially in isolation, to our knowledge, no existing framework jointly optimizes predictive guide-design models and delivery-vector design within a single pipeline a disconnect that likely underlies persistent efficacy-safety trade-offs in clinical translation. This review addresses that gap by critically synthesizing ML-driven guide design and peptide-engineered delivery within a single mechanistic and computational framework. We first outline the structural basis of peptide-derived vectors, emphasizing how charge, hydrophobicity, secondary structure, and receptor-targeting functionalization govern organ- and cell-type specificity. We then critically appraise ML methods for predicting on-target activity, off-target propensity, and specificity across CRISPR platforms, alongside computational approaches for non-coding RNA target identification, focusing on training-data limitations, feature representation, and cross-platform generalizability that constrain predictive reliability. We synthesize design principles for tissue-specific delivery, including nanocarrier integration, and highlight preclinical cases where ML-guided peptide engineering enabled targeted delivery of mRNA, antisense oligonucleotides, and CRISPR ribonucleoproteins. Finally, we assess persistent barriers data sparsity, limited model transferability, off-target genotoxicity, immunogenicity, and delivery constraints and propose emerging directions: multi-omics integration, AI-enabled de novo peptide design, and translational frameworks. This review establishes a convergent paradigm in which joint ML-guided optimization of guide and delivery design enhances the specificity, efficiency, and safety of next-generation precision genetic medicines.

title: Machine Learning-Guided Design of Peptide-Targeted CRISPR Vectors for Tissue-Specific Non-Coding RNA Knockdown.

abstract: Tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) integrate multiple microenvironmental signals, including lectin-mediated recognition of tumor-associated glycans. Although several myeloid lectins have been implicated in tumor-macrophage interactions, their contributions to immunosuppressive TAM phenotypes remain poorly defined. We implemented a CRISPR-Cas9 ribonucleoprotein (RNP) workflow in primary human monocytes to enable comparative loss-of-function interrogation of five potentially immunosuppressive lectins we previously reported. CRISPR-Cas9 RNP delivery conditions were benchmarked in freshly isolated monocytes using CD14 as a technical target, followed by sgRNA editing efficiency screening for CLEC4E, CLEC6A, CD209, SELL, and SIGLEC9 in HeLa S3 cells. Selected guides were applied to primary monocytes before co-culture in a 3D model with BT474 breast cancer cells. Editing was quantified by Sanger-sequencing deconvolution, while co-culture-derived CD45+ macrophages were isolated by fluorescence-activated cell sorting and characterized by bulk RNA sequencing. All five lectins were successfully perturbed, although gene editing efficiency remained target- and donor-dependent. Transcriptomic analysis revealed target-specific reprogramming and recurrent immunometabolic responses. mTORC1 signaling was consistently enriched, together with the remodeling of cholesterol homeostasis, fatty acid metabolism, and oxidative phosphorylation. CLEC6A deletion achieved attenuation of hypoxia-, angiogenesis-, and TNF/NF-κB-associated programs. CD209 and SIGLEC9 deletion similarly reduced hypoxia- and angiogenesis-associated signatures while promoting lipid and oxidative metabolism. CLEC4E perturbation induced broad remodeling of lipid and oxidative metabolism and stress-response, despite comparatively limited editing efficiency. Comparative lectin perturbation thus identified CLEC6A as the strongest candidate for further mechanistic investigation, while CLEC4E showed broad transcriptional remodeling despite lower editing efficiency, supporting its prioritization for improved genetic interrogation. Responses to CD209 and SIGLEC9 targeting further support tumor glycan-myeloid signaling as a regulator of TAM state. Overall, lectin perturbation redirected TAM transcriptional states through distinct immunometabolic programs rather than a uniform pro-inflammatory polarization, highlighting lectin-dependent immunometabolic regulation as a promising axis for further investigation.

title: CRISPR-Cas9 editing of myeloid lectins reveals target-dependent transcriptional remodeling in tumor-associated macrophages.

abstract: Transient RNA delivery offers a practical approach to programmable genome editing without introducing editor-encoding DNA, but editing performance depends on reagent design, delivery conditions, and target accessibility. Here, we evaluated an RNA-based editing workflow built around a cytosine base editor derived from targeted activation-induced cytidine deaminase (AID)-mediated mutagenesis (TAM). Systematic adjustment of editor mRNA and guide RNA dosage, poly(A) tail configuration, and untranslated regions identified parameters influencing cytosine-to-thymine conversion; viability remained high at 24 h under the tested RNA-dose conditions. Further optimized electroporation enabled efficient reporter mRNA delivery into primary human CD8+ T cells. In two independent donor experiments, targeted nucleotide conversion at the endogenous CD3E locus and the CD3-negative fraction were higher after sequential than after single electroporation. To investigate splice-site editing, we screened AID-Cas9 combinations targeting the mouse Nr4a2 exon 3 splice acceptor and generated mutant mice through embryo editing and subsequent breeding. Sanger sequencing of genomic DNA from primary CD8+ T cells confirmed the intended Nr4a2 splice-site mutation, while Hi-TOM-based targeted cDNA amplicon sequencing revealed altered splice-junction patterns, including the emergence of an unexpected splice junction in mutant cells. However, no statistically significant differences in tumor progression were detected in the B16-OVA adoptive transfer or B16F10 tumor models. Together, these findings provide a practical framework for transient RNA-based base editing in primary T cells and targeted modification of splice-regulatory sequences, while highlighting the complexity of splice-site editing outcomes.

title: Transient RNA-Based AID-Cas9 Editing Enables Efficient Gene and Splice-Site Modification.

abstract:
BACKGROUND/OBJECTIVES: Escherichia coli (E. coli) W3110 is a common host for recombinant protein production. However, lipopolysaccharide (LPS) endotoxin pollution brings extra challenges for downstream purification and safety testing of biotherapeutic proteins. This work set out to build low-endotoxin E. coli mutants by editing lipid A synthesis genes. We further tested their growth profiles, endotoxin levels, and ability to produce recombinant anti-vWF-A1 protein.
METHODS: The CRISPR/Cas9 genome-editing system was applied to individually and combinatorially delete lpxM and lpxL, two key genes in lipid A synthesis in E. coli W3110. We characterized bacterial growth kinetics, measured LPS endotoxin activity, expressed anti-vWF-A1 protein in wild-type and mutant strains, and quantified protein yield and residual endotoxin in purified anti-vWF-A1 preparations.
RESULTS: Three mutants, W3110ΔlpxM, W3110ΔlpxL and W3110ΔlpxMΔlpxL, were generated. Deletion of lpxL (single or combined with lpxM) extended the lag phase and decreased the maximum specific growth rate, while ΔlpxM showed only minor growth defects; all strains achieved similar final biomass. LPS endotoxin was markedly reduced in mutants, with the ΔlpxMΔlpxL double mutant showing a 92.1% reduction. When expressing anti-vWF-A1, purified protein from mutants contained significantly less endotoxin, and protein yields were comparable across strains (202-210 mg/L, 96.2-99.5% of wild-type yield).
CONCLUSIONS: Deletion of lpxM and lpxL effectively lowers endotoxin loads without substantially compromising recombinant anti-vWF-A1 productivity. This gene-editing strategy provides a feasible route to engineer low-endotoxin E. coli chassis for the manufacture of recombinant therapeutic proteins.

abstract: Neuronal excitability can be controlled by the level of potassium (K+) outside a neuron through both its effects on the cell membrane's electrical properties and its influence on ion transport across the membrane. Recent studies have also shown that certain ligand-gated ion-channel receptors can be modulated by the levels of K+ outside the neuron. Therefore, understanding how each mechanism contributes to the generation of inhibitory signals requires the ability to differentiate between them. This study represents a review that integrates evidence using various methods, including electrophysiology, structural studies, thermodynamics, and optical measurements, to propose a framework called the molecular potassium code that explains how neurons respond to varying levels of K+ in their environment. The framework describes three ways that neurons interact with changing levels of K+: how these changes shift their K+ equilibrium potential and membrane voltage; how they alter the thermodynamic driving force for KCC2-mediated cotransport of K+ and Cl-; and how receptor-dependent modulation occurs at specific receptors when documented. Changes in activation, desensitization, pharmacological sensitivity, and permeation characteristics have been measured in Drosophila DmAlka channels; however, the atomic details of K+ recognition by these channels remain unclear. Human GlyRα2 variants engineered or edited to allow for assessment of K+-associated responses under elevated K+ conditions did not provide sufficient evidence for physiological recruitment of these receptors in mammals. Additionally, the presence and function of astrocytes, as well as geometric factors such as size, shape, and orientation, affect local concentrations of K+. Therefore, the framework described here provides multiple approaches that scientists can use to measure and interpret different mechanisms contributing to the generation of inhibitory signals in the nervous system.

abstract: RNA editing is a post-transcriptional process that alters RNA nucleotide sequences, potentially affecting protein coding and RNA function. In this study, we identified 2132 senescence-associated RNA editing sites, defined as editing events present in highly senescent WI-38 fibroblasts at population doubling level (PDL) 50 but absent at earlier passages (PDL 20 or 25), by analyzing time-course bulk RNA-seq data from replicative senescence. Approximately 92% of these sites were located within Alu elements, predominantly in 3' untranslated regions (3' UTRs), suggesting widespread post-transcriptional regulatory remodeling during senescence. Numerous senescence-associated editing events exhibited elevated editing levels in tissues from older individuals in the Genotype-Tissue Expression (GTEx) project. Among these events, F11 receptor (F11R) mRNA editing was observed across multiple tissues and exhibited higher editing levels in older individuals, showing a more consistent association with aging than F11R gene expression in human tissues. These findings reveal transcriptome-wide RNA editing patterns associated with cellular senescence and suggest that RNA editing may provide a complementary layer of molecular information for studying aging and senescence-related molecular changes.

abstract: Self-amplifying vaccines based on alphavirus replicons are well established. Preclinical studies of self-amplifying vaccines based on orthoflaviviruses have also been described and include replicons based on Kunjin virus (KUNV). KUNV is an Australian subtype of West Nile virus with typically mild or asymptomatic clinical presentations in humans. Single round infectious particles (SRIPs) have emerged as an effective vaccine delivery modality for KUN replicon RNA vaccines. For instance, a SRIP vaccine encoding the glycoprotein (GP) of Zaire Ebolavirus (EBOV) was previously shown to be effective in guinea pigs and non-human primates. These SRIPs comprise self-amplifying KUN replicon RNA packaged within KUNV structural proteins, and represent virus-like-particles capable of infecting cells and delivering replicon RNA encoding an immunogen. Using EBOV GP as the model immunogen, we describe herein a novel SRIP DNA plasmid construct that illustrates a simplified in vitro methodology for the production of KUN replicon SRIPs. This SRIP DNA was also evaluated as a potential DNA vaccine; however, it performed similarly to a conventional DNA vaccine for eliciting anti-GP antibodies in Ifnar1-/- mice.

abstract: Diabetes mellitus-associated erectile dysfunction (DMED) is characterized by impaired nitric oxide signaling, microvascular injury, neuropathy, metabolic dysfunction, and cavernosal remodeling. These abnormalities may limit responses to phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors and compromise regenerative treatment. This focused narrative review examines the potential of nanotherapeutic delivery and microenvironment modulation to address these pathological barriers. We discuss catalytic nanozymes, hypoxia/reactive oxygen species-responsive neurotrophic constructs, mitochondria-targeted piezoelectric systems, fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase 1 (FBP1) mRNA-loaded lipid nanoparticles, and extracellular vesicle-hydrogel composites. By distinguishing cell experiments, interventions in diabetic animals, human observational studies, and early clinical experience with related non-nanoparticle interventions, we compare representative platforms in terms of mechanism, administration route, functional endpoints, biodistribution, duration of effect, and safety. Human functional studies provide strong evidence for impaired nitric oxide signaling, whereas therapeutic strategies targeting lactate metabolism, lactylation, ferroptosis, and mitochondrial turnover remain predominantly at the preclinical stage. We further discuss the potential value of candidate clinical phenotypes and exploratory biomarkers for future patient stratification and examine key translational challenges, including local dosing feasibility, off-target exposure, repeated-dose immunogenicity, reproductive safety, and manufacturing consistency. Overall, current findings provide a mechanistic rationale and research direction for further development of DMED nanotherapies. Further preclinical validation and clinical studies are needed to establish their efficacy, safety, and potential advantages over standard treatment.

abstract: Covalent RNA conjugates have proved effective in basic research and therapy, yet their broader use is limited by synthetic complexity and high costs. Here, we describe a modular, redox-responsive strategy for late-stage conjugation of diverse biofunctional ligands onto RNA. We show that acylation of RNA 2'-OH groups with disulfide-containing acyl moieties enables thiol-disulfide exchange with thiol-bearing ligands, including N-acetylgalactosamine (GalNAc), peptides, biotin, and captopril. The resulting conjugates undergo deconjugation under reducing conditions, tracelessly regenerating native RNA and enabling recovery of RNA function. The multivalent RNA-GalNAc construct displays preferential uptake in asialoglycoprotein receptor (ASGPR)-rich cells. Installation of biotin followed by streptavidin complexation yields bulky biotinylated RNA-streptavidin complexes that shield nuclease-sensitive RNA regions and markedly enhance the nuclease resistance of both short synthetic RNA and long messenger mRNA (mRNA). This platform may expand the chemical toolbox for RNA conjugation and support the development of functionally diverse RNA conjugates.

title: Redox-Responsive 2'-OH Acylation for Late-Stage RNA Conjugation.

abstract: mRNA-Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) for cancer vaccines are often considered a linear progression, in which formulation, biodistribution, innate stimulation, antigen expression, and tumor control form a continuum. They are not. This review connects the manufacturing inputs and lipid composition to particle attributes, innate sensing, organ and cell exposure, cytosolic translation, antigen presentation, therapeutic response, and hepatic safety. This review aims to provide a mechanism-aligned framework from critical quality attributes (CQAs) and critical process parameters (CPPs) to innate sensing, multimodal imaging, and preclinical efficacy and safety that can be used to design and interpret preclinical studies of mRNA-LNP cancer vaccines, with explicit attention to orthotopic pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) models. Principal findings: (i) total organ signal is an inadequate surrogate for productive delivery; the decisive variable is translation of antigen in a permissive antigen-presenting cell (APC) during a defined inflammatory window; (ii) formulation and process variables including size, PDI, encapsulation, RNA integrity and capping, lipid composition, PEG-lipid architecture, mixing conditions, and storage history alter this conversion; and (iii) multimodal imaging is most informative when carrier or payload tracking is paired with reporter or antigen expression, immune profiling, tumor response, and liver-safety assays. We propose a release-to-response architecture for preclinical studies and identify the evidence required for clinically interpretable pharmacology. We reviewed peer-reviewed studies on mRNA cancer vaccination, quantitative imaging, PDAC models, LNP quality-by-design, and formulation-dependent innate immunology. The total organ signal is an inadequate surrogate for productive delivery; the decisive variable is translating antigen into an antigen-presenting cell during a permissive inflammatory window. Particle size, polydispersity, encapsulation, RNA integrity and capping, lipid composition, PEG-lipid architecture, mixing conditions, and storage history can alter this conversion. Multimodal imaging is most informative when carrier or payload tracking is paired with reporter or antigen expression, immune profiling, tumor response, and liver safety assays. PDAC studies have shown that hepatic or splenic exposure can be either a liability or intentional immune reprogramming. We propose a release-to-response architecture for preclinical studies and identify the evidence required for clinically interpretable pharmacology.

title: From Formulation Quality to Anti-Tumor Immunity: A Multimodal Imaging and Translational Framework for mRNA-Lipid Nanoparticle Cancer Vaccines in Preclinical Tumor Models.

abstract: Maternal messenger RNA (mRNA) vaccination can generate maternal immunity and antibodies for passive infant protection. However, clinical evidence derives predominantly from the SARS-CoV-2 vaccines BNT162b2 and mRNA-1273, limiting generalization across the platform. This narrative review examines three questions: what determines maternal immune responses, what governs placental antibody transfer, and how immunological findings relate to infant clinical protection. Studies generally support preserved immune responsiveness during pregnancy, but associations with gestational timing are difficult to separate from dose number, previous infection, and time since antigen exposure. Transfer requires interpretation of maternal and cord-blood concentrations, because high transfer ratios do not necessarily indicate high infant antibody levels. Postnatal antibody decline and variant-dependent neutralization further limit inference from measurements at delivery. Observational studies associate maternal vaccination with reduced COVID-19-associated infant hospitalization, although residual confounding and heterogeneous exposure histories complicate comparisons between schedules. No validated infant antibody threshold predicts protection against SARS-CoV-2 infection or hospitalization. Evidence for other pathogens and self-amplifying RNA remains predominantly preclinical. Maternal immunogenicity, placental transfer, and antibody persistence therefore provide complementary evidence but cannot substitute for clinical outcomes. Future products require pregnancy-specific safety assessment and prospective studies linking maternal responses, functional antibody transfer, and postnatal persistence to clinically meaningful protection throughout infancy.

title: Maternal mRNA Vaccination: Immunological Principles and Evidence Gaps in Infant Protection.

abstract: Polygonatum zanlanscianense Pamp. is a perennial herb (Asparagaceae) endemic to China, whose rhizomes are used in folk medicine as a substitute for Polygonati Rhizoma. Although its plastome has been reported, the mitogenome remained uncharacterized. Here, we assembled and annotated the complete linear mitogenome of P. zanlanscianense and analysed its gene repertoire, codon usage, repeats, RNA editing sites, MTPTs, synteny, phylogeny and Ka/Ks. The 689,491-bp mitogenome (GC 46.23%) encodes 56 genes: 36 PCGs, three rRNA genes and 17 tRNA genes. Codon usage is biased toward A/U-ending codons. We identified 68 SSRs, 25 tandem repeats, 1366 dispersed repeat pairs, 585 predicted C-to-U editing sites concentrated at the first and second codon positions, and 30 MTPT fragments accounting for 2.24% of the mitogenome. Phylogenetic analysis placed P. zanlanscianense as sister to Polygonatum kingianum Collett & Hemsl. Median Ka/Ks was below 1 for 33 of the 35 genes analysed; although rpl5 and ccmB showed elevated ratios, branch-site tests did not support positive selection. This first mitogenome of P. zanlanscianense provides genomic resources for comparative genomic, phylogenetic and medicinal studies in Polygonatum.

abstract: Plant genome editing has been limited by the difficulty of delivering CRISPR (clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats) reagents to germline-competent cells without stable transgene integration. Viral vectors address this by exploiting endogenous replication, cell-to-cell movement and phloem transport, but cargo capacity and germline access have so far traded against each other. We classify virus-induced genome editing (VIGE) systems along two binary design choices: whether the vector itself encodes the nuclease and whether an engineered mobility mechanism carries the editing reagents to the germline. These two axes define four delivery architectures: (a) guide-only without a mobility element, in which guides are delivered into a nuclease-expressing host; (b) guide-only with a mobile RNA element that carries the guide into meristematic cells, yielding heritable edits without tissue culture; (c) nuclease-encoding without a route to the germline, achieved by shrinking the nuclease or enlarging the vector; and (d) nuclease-encoding with a mobility element, reaching the germline directly. We evaluate all four architectures against three persistent constraints. These are off-target risks from viral amplification of the editing reagents, the host range of the available vectors, and the gap between model-system demonstrations and breeding pipelines. Finally, we propose that combining engineered compact nucleases, mobile RNA signals, and morphogenic regulators could enable a single-vector pipeline for producing edited seeds. This would extend genome editing to refractory crop species and reduce reliance on tissue-culture-based transformation.

abstract: The brain is exquisitely sensitive to methyl-CpG-binding protein 2 (MeCP2) abundance. Too little causes Rett syndrome (RTT), too much causes MECP2 duplication syndrome (MDS), and in both, severity tracks with the amount of functional MeCP2. Even modest deviations are detrimental, yet how MeCP2 abundance is controlled remains poorly understood. Using genome-wide CRISPR knockout screens, we identified hundreds of proteins regulating MeCP2, revealing a casein kinase 2 alpha 1 (CSNK2A1)-driven regulatory axis stabilizing MeCP2. We show this axis is druggable and therapeutically relevant, using a novel CSNK2A1 inhibitor in human cells and targeting Csnk2a1 in an MDS mouse model. We further connect CSNK2A1-MeCP2 regulatory disruption to Okur-Chung neurodevelopmental syndrome (OCNDS), caused by mutations in CSNK2A1 , finding ∼50% less hippocampal MeCP2 in an OCNDS mouse model. Together, these data identify a druggable regulatory axis modulating MeCP2 and implicate MeCP2 dysregulation in the molecular pathogenesis of OCNDS and potentially other neurodevelopmental disorders.

title: Druggable CSNK2A1-MeCP2 regulatory axis links Okur-Chung neurodevelopmental syndrome with MECP2 -related disorders.

abstract: In vivo single-cell CRISPR screens can resolve perturbation effects in native tissues, but few combine cell-type-restricted delivery, somatic tumor initiation, and combinatorial perturbation. Here we developed an RCAS-TVA-based single-cell CRISPR screening approach coupling oncogenic transformation with single- or dual-guide perturbation in defined neural progenitors. In glioma, tumor suppressor loss produced distinct genotype-dependent transcriptional states, including an NF1 -loss-associated increase in mesenchymal programs. Introducing a fixed Cdkn2a (ARF) perturbastion altered malignant-cell state composition, immune-cell abundance, and the effects of additional tumor-suppressor perturbations, including increased representation of Pten - and Rb1 -deficient cells, suggestive of the relief of an ARF-dependent genetic barrier. These perturbations converged on transcriptional states resembling pharmacologic p53 activation in human glioblastoma. Across mouse tumors and human glioblastoma models, this response was associated with increased astrocyte-like state representation. These findings establish a framework for single-cell analysis of context-dependent somatic perturbations during tumor initiation in vivo .

title: In situ single-cell CRISPR screens uncover context-dependent rewiring of glioma states and immune recruitment.

abstract: The accelerating aging of the global population has made aging and its related diseases major public health challenges in the 21st century. Adipose tissue is not only an energy reservoir but also a crucial endocrine organ and metabolic regulator. Its dysfunction is closely linked to aging and the development of multiple diseases. This review outlines the key characteristics of adipocyte senescence and discusses its pathological contributions to obesity, type 2 diabetes, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, and cardiovascular diseases. It also summarizes current intervention strategies for adipocyte senescence, including senolytics, senomorphics, caloric restriction, physical exercise, and gene editing. We propose lipid prodrugs as promising adipose tissue delivery platforms that can be coupled with diverse therapeutic agents to increase the local concentration of drugs and minimize systemic toxicity. By utilizing the unique lipid metabolism of adipocytes, this strategy offers a new avenue for therapeutic intervention in adipocyte senescence and its associated metabolic disorders.

title: Intervening in Adipocyte Senescence: Lipid Prodrugs as an Emerging Strategy for Metabolic Disease Treatment.

abstract: Immunoglobulin A (IgA) is the most abundant antibody isotype produced by mammals, and has a specialized role in mucosal homeostasis1. IgA is constantly secreted into the intestinal lumen and binds to commensal microorganisms to regulate their colonization and function2,3, with unclear implications for health. IgA deficiency is common in humans, but difficult to study, because of its complex aetiology and comorbidities4-8. Here we use genetically and environmentally controlled mice to show that various models of IgA deficiency result in increased susceptibility to several models of endogenous colorectal cancer. Cellular and molecular analyses revealed that, in the absence of IgA, colonic epithelial cells induce antibacterial factors and accelerate cell cycling in response to the microbiota. Oral treatment with IgA was sufficient to reduce steady-state proliferation and protect mice from tumours; however, this function was due to the structure of the antibody rather than to binding specificity. In a reductionist culture system, IgA directly suppressed epithelial growth. Co-immunoprecipitation mass spectrometry and targeted CRISPR screening identified DMBT1 as an IgA-binding epithelial surface protein that is required for IgA-mediated suppression of proliferation. Together, IgA and DMBT1 tune the normal cycling of absorptive colonocyte progenitors. In IgA-knockout mice, deleting the transmembrane and cytoplasmic signalling portions of DMBT1 was sufficient to reverse both the increased epithelial cell proliferation and the increased tumour susceptibility seen in these mice. These experiments establish a homeostatic function for IgA in tempering physiological epithelial responses to the microbiota to maintain mucosal health.

abstract: Simultaneous detection of dual microRNA biomarkers is crucial for accurate prognosis and treatment monitoring of cervical spondylosis, yet remains challenging due to the lack of stringent logic control and high-fidelity signal amplification. Herein, we report an AND-gate-controlled colorimetric assay that integrates target-recycling strand displacement amplification, CRISPR/Cas13a/crRNA-mediated trans-cleavage, and self-priming cyclic amplification for sensitive and specific analysis of two cervical spondylosis-associated miRNAs (miRNA-221 and miRNA-146a). Only when both targets are present does the cascade proceed, producing double-stranded amplicons that trigger SYBR Green I-catalyzed TMB oxidation, yielding a naked-eye-visible blue signal. The assay exhibits a broad linear range from 10 fM to 500 pM, a detection limit of 2.12 fM, excellent selectivity, and good repeatability. Importantly, we applied this method to clinically evaluate the therapeutic effect of auricular point pressing (ear acupressure), a traditional Chinese medicine intervention for cervical spondylosis. In a 4-week study of 20 patients, the treatment group receiving auricular point pressing showed significant downregulation of both miRNAs compared to baseline, while the control group showed no notable change. Results correlated well with RT-qPCR, confirming reliability. This logic-controlled CRISPR/Cas13a platform offers a robust, equipment-free strategy for early prognosis of cervical spondylosis and objective monitoring of auricular point pressing therapy.
